index.title: Which Value Takes the Blame
index.prompt: Change the loss of the head 1 example: it is now the sum of the first numbers of all three head 1 outputs, those of "the", "cat" and "sat". In head 1, "the" puts weight 1.000 on itself, "cat" puts 0.250 on "the" and 0.750 on itself, and "sat" puts 0.115 on "the", 0.709 on "cat" and 0.175 on itself. Training passes the gradient back to the three values of head 1. Which value gets the largest gradient on its first number?
index.answer: The value of "cat". Here dO has a 1 in the first column of every row, so dV = $A^\top dO$ puts in each value's first column the sum of the weights that all three tokens put on it, a column sum of A: 1.000 + 0.250 + 0.115 = 1.365 for "the", 0.750 + 0.709 = 1.459 for "cat" and 0.175 for "sat". A value is blamed for every output it feeds, in proportion to the weight each output gives it, and two tokens put large weights on "cat".

index.title: One Wide Head in Place of Two
index.prompt: Keep the running example's tables W_Q, W_K and W_V, but use them as one head of 4 numbers in place of two heads of 2: each query is compared with each key over all four numbers. Step 5 gives the scores of “sat” as 0.721, 2.539 and 1.142 in head 1 and 1.120, 0.961 and 2.950 in head 2. With the causal mask as before, what weight does “sat” put on “cat”?
index.answer: 0.353. A dot product over four numbers is head 1's dot product plus head 2's. Multiplying the scores of “sat” from Step 5 back by √2 gives its dot products: 1.020, 3.591 and 1.615 in head 1, and 1.584, 1.359 and 4.172 in head 2. Their sums, 2.604, 4.950 and 5.787, divided by the square root of 4, are the scores 1.302, 2.475 and 2.894, and the softmax gives 0.109, 0.353 and 0.537. The single head splits its weight between “cat” and “sat” itself, so its output is a blend that neither head gives on its own.

Training passes the gradient back to the three values of head 1. Which value gets the largest gradient on its first number?

choices.text: All three get the same gradient
choices.explain: Each row of the weights adds up to 1, but a row sum is what A times dO would give. The gradient of a value is $A^\top dO$: look at what each value collects from all the tokens that use it, which is a column of A, not a row.

Every token attends to "the", but counting the tokens that use a value is not enough. The gradient adds up the weights those tokens put on it, and two of the three weights on "the" are small. Add up each column of the weights before comparing.

A value is blamed for every output it feeds, in proportion to the weight each output gives it, and two tokens put large weights on "cat".

theory.title: One Wide Head in Place of Two

prompt.p: Keep the running example's tables $W_Q$, $W_K$ and $W_V$, but use them as one head of 4 numbers in place of two heads of 2: each query is compared with each key over all four numbers. This adds the two heads' scores, 1.841, 3.500 and 4.092, which keeps the divisor √2 of a head of 2. The scale belongs to the head that computes the score, so work out what a head of 4 numbers divides its dot products by.

This averages the two heads' weights on “cat”, 0.709 and 0.105. One head computes one set of scores and one softmax: the dot products of the two halves add before the softmax, and a softmax of summed scores is not the average of two softmaxes.

That is head 1's weight. One head cannot keep head 1's pattern and ignore the numbers head 2 used: they are now part of the same dot product, and they favor “sat” itself, with a dot product of 4.172 against 1.359 for “cat”.
